rounds.proof_sketch: The removed __syncthreads() at line 130 occurs after mean computation (mean = shared_sum[0] / spatial_size) and before the variance loop. The preceding mean reduction loop ends with __syncthreads() when stride=1, guaranteeing all threads see shared_sum[0]. Between mean read and next shared memory write (shared_sq_sum[tid] = sq_sum), no thread modifies shared_sum[]. Since 65536/256=256 iterations per thread with no early exits, all threads follow identical control flow. The sync was provably redundant.
rounds.survival_reason: The removed synchronization barrier was functionally unnecessary. After the mean reduction loop completes, all threads are already synchronized by the loop's final __syncthreads() call. At that point, shared_sum[0] contains the computed sum and no thread ever writes to it again before the variance computation begins. Each thread reads shared_sum[0] independently to compute its local mean variable, then performs the variance accumulation using only global memory reads and local variable writes. The next shared memory operation (shared_sq_sum[tid] = sq_sum) is properly protected by its own subsequent __syncthreads(). Therefore, no race condition or memory visibility issue can occur regardless of input values.
rounds.kill_strategy: Unkillable. The removed __syncthreads() protected no actual memory hazard. The shared_sum array is not modified after the reduction loop ends, and all threads have already synchronized at that point. No input value pattern can create a race condition that doesn't exist in the memory access pattern.
rounds.recommendations: When adding __syncthreads() for safety, document whether each barrier is strictly necessary or defensive. Mutation testing tools could benefit from static analysis that detects 'orphan' syncs that don't actually separate conflicting shared memory accesses, marking such sync removals as likely equivalent mutations.
